title: What If We Stopped Starting Over
author: Melinda Karshner
summary: Karshner, a 15-year veteran teacher, argues that American reading-curriculum reform follows a destructive pattern: each new pendulum swing discards everything from the prior era instead of isolating and fixing the specific components that failed, the way engineers refine one broken part rather than replacing an entire system. She traces this pattern historically through the 1990s-2000s Open Court Reading adoption, showing that a 2007 study of teachers' complaints about Open Court reads almost identically to 2025 teacher complaints about current Science of Reading basals like Into Reading and Wonders. Karshner contends that both Balanced Literacy and phonics-heavy scripted programs contained genuine strengths worth preserving, and that treating either era as wholly villainous prevents districts from doing the harder work of refinement. Her proposed fix centers on sustained, multi-year teacher training that outlives any single curriculum adoption, so that mastery of reading pedagogy becomes portable across programs rather than dependent on fidelity to a particular box.
points: Karshner's central diagnosis is structural, not partisan: education throws the whole thing out and starts from scratch every eight years instead of isolating which specific component of a program failed, unlike engineering disciplines that refine one broken part.

She uses a striking historical parallel—a 2007 study of teacher complaints about Open Court Reading matches near word-for-word the 2025 complaints about Into Reading and Wonders—to argue the field keeps repeating an already-documented failure mode.

Her argument resists tribal curriculum politics on both sides: she credits Balanced Literacy for volume of authentic reading and phonics-heavy basals for strong explicit instruction, while criticizing what each discarded.

The proposed fix is teacher-training infrastructure rather than a new curriculum: multi-year professional development robust enough that teachers can teach reading with any program, or with none, making expertise outlast any single adoption cycle.
quotes: Every discipline that improves does it the same way. You keep what works, you isolate the part that doesn't, and you revise that part. NASA engineers do not throw out entire Mars rovers. They observe, they analyze, they figure out which component failed, and they fix that component.

For whatever reason, education does not work this way. Education throws the whole thing out and starts from scratch. Or rather, it pretends to start from scratch while actually grabbing onto the same thing that didn't work eight years ago.

For example, this 2007 study on teachers' perceptions of the basal program Open Court could easily be swapped out for 2025 teacher rhetoric regarding popular basals of today, such as Into Reading and Wonders.

Teachers felt Open Court's rapid instructional pace and lack of meaningful interaction led students to tune out. Teachers also noted that the program's guidance for differentiating instruction for English learners was not helpful in practice.

What students need instead is deep, multi-year teacher training that leaves teachers able to teach reading with any program, or with none. Scripted programs are great for teachers who are still learning on their path to mastery. But they are a crutch, and eventually every teacher should be able to run without them.
Fidelity to best practice will always win over fidelity to any box.
